item.title: Un avión resulta dañado en el aeropuerto de Riad por ataques hutíes, dicen fuentes
item.description: Los hutíes de Yemen, alineados con Irán, intensificaron su letal campaña de ataques contra Arabia Saudita, con el objetivo de bloquear el espacio aéreo y las instalaciones petroleras del reino mediante lanzamientos de misiles que han causado la muerte de tres personas esta semana y han dejado un avión gravemente dañado.
item.dc:creator: Timour Azhari, Federico Maccioni
item.content:encoded: Los hutíes de Yemen, alineados con Irán, intensificaron su letal campaña de ataques contra Arabia Saudita, con el objetivo de bloquear el espacio aéreo y las instalaciones petroleras del reino mediante lanzamientos de misiles que han causado la muerte de tres personas esta semana y han dejado un avión gravemente dañado. El grupo dijo que había atacado el aeropuerto de Riad y advirtió a los trabajadores de que se mantuvieran alejados de las centrales energéticas, que serían objeto de ataques. La metralla procedente de una interceptación o del impacto de otro proyectil había dejado gravemente dañado el avión comercial perteneciente a la aerolínea estatal saudita Saudia Airlines tras incendiarse mientras estaba estacionado en una terminal del aeropuerto el jueves, dijeron tres personas informadas sobre el asunto. Las fuentes dijeron que, según se cree, no había pasajeros a bordo del avión en ese momento, pero no pudieron descartar que haya habido heridos como consecuencia del incidente. En un vídeo verificado por Reuters se veía una espesa columna negra de humo y llamas elevándose desde el aeropuerto de Riad. La oficina de prensa del Gobierno de Arabia Saudita, su autoridad de aviación civil y Saudia Airlines no respondieron a las solicitudes de comentarios enviadas por correo electrónico. Lufthansa y Air India anunciaron que suspendían los vuelos a Riad tras los ataques de los hutíes. Por otra parte, las autoridades sauditas dijeron que los restos de un misil interceptado habían impactado en una guardería y un complejo médico de Riad. Los hutíes afirman que están atacando al reino por su apoyo a las fuerzas gubernamentales en la reavivada guerra civil de Yemen. Arabia Saudita ha dicho que respalda una ofensiva del Gobierno yemení reconocido por la ONU para recuperar territorio de manos de los hutíes. El conflicto, que ahora se ha convertido en una extensión de la guerra entre Estados Unidos e Irán, ha añadido un nuevo caos a una región ya en llamas y amenaza con arrastrar a otros Estados a una agotadora lucha en las montañas, mientras Siria se plantea ahora desplegar tropas para ayudar a Arabia Saudita.

item.title: Campanha de Flávio nega privatização de estatais e promete fortalecer programas sociais e reduzir impostos
item.description: O coordenador da área econômica da campanha à Presidência de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), Adolfo Sachsida, negou nesta quinta-feira que, se eleito, o senador privatizará estatais como Banco do Brasil, Caixa Econômica Federal e Petrobras, e prometeu que um eventual governo Flávio irá "fortalecer" programas sociais como o Bolsa Família e o Benefício de Prestação Continuada (BPC) ao mesmo tempo que reduzirá impostos.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: O coordenador da área econômica da campanha à Presidência de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), Adolfo Sachsida, negou nesta quinta-feira que, se eleito, o senador privatizará estatais como Banco do Brasil, Caixa Econômica Federal e Petrobras, e prometeu que um eventual governo Flávio irá "fortalecer" programas sociais como o Bolsa Família e o Benefício de Prestação Continuada (BPC) ao mesmo tempo que reduzirá impostos. Em vídeo publicado em sua conta no X, Sachsida disse que o ajuste fiscal prometido pelo candidato "será focado nos excessos do governo" e citou redução no número de ministérios e salários de funcionários públicos que, em alguns casos, segundo ele, chegam a R$200 mil. "Nós vamos preservar todos os programas sociais, e não é só preservar, não, nós vamos fortalecer os programas sociais. Então, se você que está vendo esse vídeo recebe o Bolsa Família, o BPC, pode ter certeza que nós vamos respeitar, e muito, você e sua família e vamos fortalecer esses programas todos", disse. "Se você que está vendo esse vídeo é um empresário, saiba que nós vamos reduzir impostos, vamos reduzir burocracia, vamos facilitar a sua vida", prometeu. Sachsida, que foi ministro de Minas e Energia no governo Jair Bolsonaro e secretário de Política Econômica do ministro da Economia de Bolsonaro, Paulo Guedes, negou ainda que Flávio pretenda privatizar estatais. "Se você que está ouvindo esse vídeo é do Banco do Brasil, da Caixa Econômica e da Petrobras saiba de uma coisa: não existirão privatizações de empresas. Nenhuma dessas empresas será tocada", disse. Mais cedo, o jornal Folha de S.Paulo publicou reportagem em que afirma que a equipe de Flávio estuda, caso ele seja eleito, mudar a correção dos benefícios da Previdência e do BPC, assim como dos gastos obrigatórios em saúde e educação, com objetivo de obter um corte de R$250 bilhões. Em seu vídeo, Sachsida não menciona a matéria do jornal, mas pede aos seguidores que não acreditem em "fake news". "Nós vamos colocar as contas públicas em ordem respeitando a população brasileira. Então não acredite em fake news".

item.title: Thousands of Spaniards march to mark death of octogenarian at heart of housing protests
item.description: Thousands of Spaniards marched through central Madrid on Thursday to mark the death of the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her home ignited protests across the country and led to a snap election next month.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Thousands of Spaniards marched through central Madrid on Thursday to mark the death of the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her home ignited protests across the country and led to a snap election next month. Maricarmen Abascal, who died on Wednesday, had been hospitalised for severe anxiety and exhaustion since her [USN:L8N45F0PQ TEXT:" eviction"] on September 23. No cause of death has been announced. Protests over home shortages and surging rents following her eviction prompted Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call a snap [USN:L8N45R05N TEXT:"general election"] for November 29 after parliament rejected his government's proposals to address a mounting housing crisis. As the sun set in Madrid, thousands followed a line of Tenants Union members, dressed in orange vests and walking arm-in-arm, as they carried a wreath of flowers from a protest camp in central Puerta del Sol square to Abascal's former home near Retiro Park. "They're not deaths; they're murders," the protesters chanted. Several people who received eviction orders have died by suicide in Spain in recent months. Political leaders on Thursday traded blame and invoked Abascal's case in attacks on opponents. Left-leaning parties criticised conservatives who [USN:L1N45O0BD TEXT:"rejected"] legislation in parliament aimed at curbing soaring rental prices. Right-wingers said the leftist central government had been unable to tackle the crisis after eight years in power. Alberto Nuñez Feijoo, leader of the conservative opposition People's Party (PP), accused Sanchez and the Socialists of trying to exploit the housing crisis for political gain before the election. "We will not allow this attempt to manipulate the emotions of the Spanish people; all of this has happened during their eight years in government. It won’t fly," Feijoo said. In the Madrid regional assembly, opposition leader Manuela Bergerot of the leftist Mas Madrid party said Maricarmen — as she has become known across Spain — had died because of "miserable people who put gain above a person's life." She said the last thing Madrid regional leader Isabel Diaz Ayuso had done while Maricarmen was alive was "laugh at her" — a reference to Ayuso's quip on September 28: "At what age do I get to stop paying my landlords? Let me know." Ayuso blamed Sanchez, saying Maricarmen had been evicted under his government. PROTESTERS BLAME 'GREEDY' LANDLORDS News of the octogenarian's death enraged protesters camped on squares in Spain's main cities who chanted that she had been "murdered" because of the greed of her landlords. After an investment fund purchased the building where she had lived for more than 70 years, Abascal lost a lengthy legal battle against rent increases far beyond her pension income, leading to her eviction. While in hospital, she reached a deal to regain her home but she died before she could return. "When everything is private, we will be deprived of everything," said a placard on Puerta del Sol square, where mourners lit candles and left flowers honouring Maricarmen. Outside Abascal's building, mourners left flowers, candles, handwritten notes and children's drawings. "Maricarmen was the straw that broke the camel's back... (she was) a symbol of resistance and unity," said Alex Marinero, a 21-year-old protester. Tributes to Abascal in the Madrid region's legislature also caused arguments as lawmakers accused each other of cynically exploiting the case. The PP, which has absolute majorities in the Madrid regional and local assemblies, refused to hold a minute of silence honouring her. Instead, hard-left deputies staged one outside City Hall and gave Abascal a 60-second standing ovation during a tense debate in the regional assembly, while PP lawmakers remained seated with folded arms. A survey carried out in June and published by state pollster CIS on Thursday found 76.3% of Spaniards supported intervention in the market to guarantee access to housing, while 79% believe the right to housing should take precedence over treating homes as a market commodity. Ombudsman Angel Gabilondo said addressing the housing crisis would require greater commitment from all levels of government. He said his office was preparing a housing report and reiterated proposals including expanding public housing, restricting tourist rentals, increasing rent assistance and strengthening protections against evictions for vulnerable households.

item.title: Argenx discontinues Vyvgart study in Sjögren's disease, shares tumble
item.description: Argenx said on Thursday it had discontinued a late-stage study of its efgartigimod drug in adults with Sjögren's disease, an autoimmune condition that damages the glands producing tears and saliva, putting its shares on track for their biggest one-day fall in almost three years.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Argenx (ARGX.BR) said on Thursday it had discontinued a late-stage study of its efgartigimod drug in adults with Sjögren's disease, an autoimmune condition that damages the glands producing tears and saliva, putting its shares on track for their biggest one-day fall in almost three years. The drug, commercialized under Vyvgart, has become one of Europe's most successful biotech launches through its use in treatment of two other autoimmune diseases, and Argenx sees rheumatology as a potential new growth platform for it. Sjögren's is primarily diagnosed and treated by rheumatologists. An independent data monitoring committee recommended stopping the study after an interim analysis concluded the study was unlikely to meet its primary endpoint Sjögren's has a high unmet need and no approved treatment, so analysts had seen the trials as a clear opportunity for Vyvgart The shares were down 16% by 1109 GMT, wiping off €8.5 billion ($9.5 billion) from Argenx's market value The stock is by far the biggest faller on Europe's downbeat healthcare index (.SXDP) , which fell 1.8% ($1 = 0.8942 euros)

item.title: S&P 500, Nasdaq end lower as crude prices jump, chip stocks weigh
item.description: US stocks dipped on Thursday as crude prices surged on a spike in Middle East tensions and a cut in US output that stoked inflation and rate-hike fears, while semiconductor stocks slumped.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Culp, Tharuniyaa Lakshmi
item.content:encoded: US stocks dipped on Thursday as crude prices surged on a spike in Middle East tensions and a cut in US output that stoked inflation and rate-hike fears, while semiconductor stocks slumped. Of the major US stock indexes, the Nasdaq closed with the steepest percentage loss, two days after the tech-heavy index reached a record closing high. The S&P 500's loss was more modest, while the blue-chip Dow eked out a nominal gain. Chipmakers (.SOX) , which have soared over 80% so far this year, were clear underperformers on the day, falling 3.4% in the wake of a report from the Financial Times that OpenAI's annualized revenues were $20 billion less than the company previously signaled. "The market's going sideways in anticipation of third-quarter earnings season, which begins next week, and then there's the ongoing conflict in Iran that's pushing oil prices higher," said Terry Sandven, chief equity strategist at US Bank Wealth Management in Minneapolis, Minnesota. "What's equally telling is that year-to-date, the path of least resistance for equities has been up." [USN:L1N45U031 TEXT:"Oil prices"] jumped on supply concerns after a spate of attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, combined with a cut in US output due to hurricane activity. Front-month WTI and Brent settled up 3.6% and 4.1%, respectively. Tight global crude supplies during the Iran war have sent US crude soaring more than 60% so far this year, stoking inflation pressures. In response to those pressures, the US Federal Reserve hiked interest rates in September for the first time since July 2023. Financial markets currently expect the central bank to leave rates unchanged this month, while the probability of a December hike is 69.2%, according to CME's FedWatch tool. That mirrors the expected rate hike path of the [USN:L6N45U0QU TEXT:"European Central Bank"], and was affirmed by Fed Governor [USN:L6N45T15S TEXT:"Christopher Waller"], who said additional rate hikes will probably be necessary, but the timing of those hikes is "flexible." The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) rose 51.77 points, or 0.10%, to 51,231.64, the S&P 500 (.SPX) lost 36.41 points, or 0.47%, to 7,765.36 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) lost 345.35 points, or 1.25%, to 27,193.34. Among the 11 major sectors in the S&P 500, energy stocks (.SPNY) led the percentage gainers, while technology (.SPLRCT) , weighed by chips, suffered the steepest loss. Memory-chip giant Samsung Electronics' (005930.KS) record quarterly profit forecast failed to lift sentiment, with its shares closing lower in South Korea. Rival Micron Technology (MU.O) dropped 4.8%. On Wednesday, the Wall Street Journal reported that [USN:FWN45T25Y TEXT:"Broadcom"] (AVGO.O) is lining up $50 billion in financing for OpenAI, with Oracle (ORCL.N) also seeking an unspecified sum, spurring fears that massive debt issuance by technology companies could intensify the competition for capital. Broadcom and Oracle fell 4.4% and 5.5%, respectively. [USN:L6N45U0N9 TEXT:"PepsiCo"] (PEP.O) shares gained 3.7% after the beverage company said it would pursue additional spending cuts while lowering its annual core profit forecast. [USN:L6N45U0YO TEXT:"Starbucks"] (SBUX.O) dipped 0.4% following reports that the coffee chain was exploring a purchase of Chipotle Mexican Grill (CMG.N) , whose shares jumped 6.2%. Palantir (PLTR.O) climbed 2.4% after Goldman Sachs upgraded its rating on the data analytics software provider to "buy" from "neutral." Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.28-to-1 ratio on the NYSE. There were 110 new highs and 416 new lows on the NYSE. On the Nasdaq, 2,050 stocks rose and 2,734 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.33-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 4 new 52-week highs and 12 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 33 new highs and 319 new lows. Volume on US exchanges was 18.81 billion shares, compared with the 17.74 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days.

item.title: UK's ASOS says cyber hack accessed customers' personal data
item.description: British online fashion retailer ASOS said on Thursday that a cybersecurity breach earlier this week had exposed some customers' personal information, including names and contact details, according to its initial investigation.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: British online fashion retailer ASOS (ASOS.L) said on Thursday that a [USN:L6N45S0OD TEXT:"cybersecurity breach"] earlier this week had exposed some customers' personal information, including names and contact details, according to its initial investigation. It said the hacker also had access to "certain non-personal account related information," but no payment card information or account passwords, ASOS said in an email to customers. "We discovered that an unauthorised party gained access to an ASOS employee account by impersonating a trusted contact to obtain log in credentials," ASOS said. "Those credentials were then used to access information on certain third-party platforms used by ASOS." It said the affected platforms were immediately locked down, ensuring that no further information could be accessed, adding that the ASOS website and app were safe to use throughout, and remain safe to use. ASOS said it is working with the relevant law enforcement and regulatory authorities. Shares in ASOS were up 3%, paring losses for the week to 8%. So-called "social engineering" operations, where hackers impersonate workers to gain access to companies' computer networks, are prevalent. British companies and institutions have been increasingly hit by aggressive and regular cyber and ransomware attacks in recent years. The British Library, a blood testing service, the London Underground, Marks & Spencer (MKS.L) , the Co-op and Jaguar Land Rover are some that have suffered months of disruption due to such breaches.

item.title: Kingspan hit with €40 million EU fine for misleading data on Slovenian deal
item.description: Irish building materials maker Kingspan was fined €40 million ($44.7 million) for providing incorrect and misleading information during an investigation into its abandoned acquisition of a Slovenian rival, EU antitrust regulators said on Thursday.
item.dc:creator: Yun Chee Foo
item.content:encoded: Irish building materials maker Kingspan (KRX.I) was fined €40 million ($44.7 million) for providing incorrect and misleading information during an investigation into its abandoned acquisition of a Slovenian rival, EU antitrust regulators said on Thursday. The sanction followed a four-year investigation by the European Commission, which is the European Union competition enforcer, and underscores its tough policy against such infringements of EU merger rules. Kingspan said it would challenge the EU fine. "We look forward to appealing the decision in full," the company said in an email. EU antitrust chief Teresa Ribera said companies must adhere to merger rules. "When companies withhold or distort the truth, they undermine a system that protects fair competition for everyone. There can be no compromise on disclosure and transparency. If they fail to do so, we do and will act firmly," she said in a statement. Kingspan announced its plan to acquire Trimo in 2021 but scrapped the deal in April 2022 after the EU antitrust watchdog warned that the acquisition could jack up prices and reduce quality. The Commission subsequently opened an investigation in November 2022 to examine whether Kingspan had provided incorrect and misleading information. Its Thursday decision said the company provided misleading information about how it tracks penetration rates for mineral fibre sandwich panels and the availability of bidding data, as well as incorrect information about board members' involvement in certain matters. Such breaches can cost companies fines up to 1% of their total global turnover. ($1 = 0.8940 euros)

item.title: TSX rebounds from 2-1/2-month low as oil climbs
item.description: Canada's main stock index clawed back some of the previous day's steep decline on Thursday as a jump in oil prices boosted energy shares.

item.content:encoded: Canada's main stock index clawed back some of the previous day's steep decline on Thursday as a jump in oil prices boosted energy shares. The Toronto Stock Exchange's S&P/TSX Composite Index (.GSPTSE) ended up 103.52 points, or 0.3%, at 35,145.38, after on Wednesday falling 1.7% to its lowest closing level since July 20. "People are reacting to the increased tensions in the Middle East," said Michael Sprung, president at Treegrove Investment Management. "There's a lot to be concerned about in this environment," Sprung said, pointing to elevated oil prices and interest rates, as well as uncertainty around midterm elections in the United States. Government borrowing costs globally have climbed in recent weeks on heightened worries about inflation and rising interest rates, along with nagging anxiety about nations' debt loads. [USN:L1N45U031 TEXT:"US crude oil futures"] settled 3.6% higher at $91.49 a barrel on revived concerns about the ongoing war in the Middle East and growing supply disruptions due to a hurricane approaching the US Gulf Coast. Energy (.SPTTEN) rose 2.8% and the materials group, which includes metal mining shares, ended 0.7% higher. [USN:L1N45U0TG TEXT:"Gold"] rebounded from a two-month low as investors weighed the Federal Reserve's uncertain interest-rate path against growing concerns over high levels of US debt. [USN:L1N45T0ZJ TEXT:"Richelieu Hardware"] (RCH.TO) was a standout. The hardware distributor's shares jumped 11.4% after the company reported increased third-quarter revenue. Four of the 10 major sectors ended lower, including technology (.SPTTTK) . It lost 1.1% and heavily weighted financials (.SPTTFS) were down 0.3%.

item.title: Zelenskiy accuses US of inaction as Russian strikes kill over 70 in two days
item.description: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy accused the US of being unwilling to help Ukraine after a Russian bomb attack on Thursday killed at least 35 people in the east, sending the two-day death toll from Russian strikes to over 70.
item.dc:creator: Yuliia Dysa, Max Hunder
item.content:encoded: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy accused the US of being unwilling to help Ukraine after a Russian bomb attack on Thursday killed at least 35 people in the east, sending the two-day death toll from Russian strikes to over 70. Hours after the strike on the embattled city of Kramatorsk tore through two buses, Zelenskiy criticised Washington's effort to pursue economic ties with Russia while also seeking to mediate the more than four-year war. City authorities reported a new drone attack in the evening that killed two people. That brought to 35 the total death toll in the city. Local authorities reported that a Russian guided aerial bomb killed two people in a village in southeastern Dnipropetrovsk and one person died in the western city of Ivano-Frankivsk. The attacks were launched a day after a mass Russian drone and missile assault killed dozens across Ukraine — 22 of them in a residential building in the central town of Pryluky, around 130 km (80 miles) east of Kyiv. Speaking in the early evening, Zelenskiy said 78 people were killed and 215 wounded by strikes in the last two days across Ukraine. Speaking to reporters in Pryluky, the Ukrainian leader urged the US to accede to his requests to expand Ukraine's access to the Starlink satellite service to help it target Russian ballistic-missile launchers. 'THAT'S CALLED UNWILLINGNESS' "Open Starlink for Ukraine. You did open it when you were responding to Iran ... I’ve said quite openly — give it to us, help us defend our skies and dominate there. And then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table," he said in an emotional statement. Ukraine has in recent months aimed to wrest the battlefield initiative from Russia, whose gains have slowed this year, but is still suffering from Moscow's increasingly brutal air war. "So where's the truth here, where's the honesty? Where's the stalemate? ... That's called unwillingness," he said, referring to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's assertion earlier on Thursday the war is at [USN:L1N45U0GU TEXT:"a stalemate"] and that the United States would keep working toward a settlement. "One cannot, on the one hand, negotiate with the Russians about future economic projects, whilst on the other hand say that we find ourselves in some sort of ... diplomatic stalemate," Zelenskiy added. Top Russian and US officials, including US Special Envoy Jared Kushner, have [USN:L8N45G0SP TEXT:"held talks"] about bringing a US investor into the Nord Stream pipelines that delivered Russian gas to Germany before Moscow invaded Ukraine, Reuters reported on Thursday. Ukrainian negotiators will travel to the US on Friday and Saturday for talks, Zelenskiy added, urging US President Donald Trump to increase sanction pressure on Russia. Zelenskiy told reporters in Kyiv that he expected Kyiv's European partners to join the talks with the US. He also said Ukrainian negotiators would raise the issue of air defences in light of near-constant Russian attacks. INTENSIFYING STRIKES Twenty people were wounded in the Kramatorsk strike — one of the biggest single attacks of the year by Russia. Moscow has denied targeting civilians, but regularly pounds cities with missiles and drones. "The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians. For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible," regional governor Vadym Filashkin said on the Telegram app. Images posted by officials showed bodies strewn across a street littered with debris and a charred shell of a bus. Some bodies had not been identified yet, Zelenskiy said, adding that the attack would not go unanswered. Separately, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said four people were killed and 19 wounded in morning attacks on the Ukrainian capital Kyiv. Water and electricity supplies were subject to interruptions which officials said would take time to put right. Russia has unleashed relentless drone strikes against Kyiv in recent weeks, targeting warehouses, data centres and renewing its campaign against Ukraine's power grid ahead of winter. Russian technology and AI company Yandex [USN:L8N45U1P7 TEXT:"said"] it could not yet determine whether equipment at a data centre hit by a Ukrainian drone attack could be restored. Zelenskiy did not refer specifically to the strike on Yandex, but said Ukraine was "mirroring" Russian attacks on data centres.

item.title: French students keep up protest pressure with some demonstrations hit by violence
item.description: French teenagers blockaded some high schools and marched through cities on Thursday in the latest wave of nationwide protests about conditions in the country's schools, and some of the demonstrations were marred by violent unrest.
item.dc:creator: Manon Cruz, Dominique Vidalon
item.content:encoded: French teenagers blockaded some high schools and marched through cities on Thursday in the latest wave of nationwide protests about conditions in the country's schools, and some of the demonstrations were marred by violent unrest. The Interior Ministry said 71,500 people participated in the day's demonstrations, of which 24,500 took part in the main Paris protest centred around the Bastille square. The Paris protest was mostly peaceful, although there were occasional clashes between small groups of demonstrators and the police during the evening. Elsewhere, arsonists attacked a [USN:FWN45U1T1 TEXT:"Bordeaux"] police station, a school in Saint-Etienne was ransacked and a teacher in Toulouse was hit by a demonstrator, said the Interior Ministry. In Marseille, police said a teacher at Victor Hugo High School [USN:FWN45U1T4 TEXT:"was attacked"] during the latest protests and has filed a criminal complaint over the incident. A banner reads: "Funding cut, youth sacrificed." REUTERS/Manon Cruz The protest movement, now into its third week, has exposed deep tensions in France between popular demands for investments in deteriorating public services and a cash-strapped government under [USN:L8N45S1P0 TEXT:"pressure from bond markets"] to reduce its debt and deficit. Protesters say they are demonstrating to demand more teachers and better facilities, arguing school buildings are often dilapidated, with overcrowded classrooms that are often freezing in winter and boiling in summer. Critics say the movement has been infiltrated by violent far-left and anarchist elements. High-school teacher Diane Di Sciullo joined students in Marseille, saying all they were asking for was a decent education in decent conditions. She denounced overcrowding, saying this year she had 37 students in her class. "At the start of every lesson, I have to ask them to check the neighbouring classrooms for spare chairs and desks so they can actually study," she said. Di Sciullo, 28, was carrying a placard that read, "I'm a teacher and my students help me catch cockroaches in class." MINISTER PROMISES URGENT ACTION Education ministry figures showed the number of school blockades was gradually decreasing. Education Minister Edouard Geffray told TF1 TV that extra teachers would be drafted in to plug gaps in schools which do not have enough teachers, while heavy school timetables will also be reviewed. It is not uncommon for French teenagers to have lessons from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., as well as large amounts of homework. Geffray also said he was working on potential improvements to Parcoursup, the national online portal for applying to university, which has been widely criticised as confusing and stressful for applicants. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu pledged late on Wednesday that the government would present "concrete, quick and fully funded responses" to the protests by late October, without offering specifics. Student protest leaders said that was not good enough and called for further marches next Tuesday. There are also calls circulating online for a day of protests on October 17. "Our demands must be heard. Yesterday, Mr Lecornu gave us a lot of hot air," said Ryad Rani, leader of one of the student unions. "The mobilisation will continue, we're not backing down on anything." A prominent complaint featured on banners and placards was that the police response to the wave of protests has been too heavy-handed. "Too young to be listened to, old enough to be tear-gassed" was one example. There have been hundreds of arrests and dozens of injuries since the movement started. On Wednesday, the government [USN:L1N45T0EM TEXT:"suspended the use of stun grenades"] in the policing of the protests after one [USN:L1N45R08Q TEXT:"teenager's hand was blown off"]. POLITICAL RESPONSE SHOWS POLARISATION AS ELECTION LOOMS Six months from a presidential election, the protests have highlighted stark polarisation between leading candidates to replace Emmanuel Macron, who cannot seek a third term. Far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen has highlighted damage to schools caused by a minority of protesters and outlined [USN:L8N45R1J6 TEXT:"plans to slash public spending"] should she win. Her hard-left opponent Jean-Luc Melenchon, who also has a chance of making the runoff, has praised the protesters as "incredible" and denounced police brutality. According to an Elabe poll for BFM TV, 72% of French people think the students' demands are legitimate, but 55% of them think the protests should stop. Neighbouring [USN:L1N45T0NH TEXT:"Belgium"] has also had student protests, with demonstrations in Brussels, Ciney and Liege.

item.title: Denmark plans ban on sharing AI deepfakes without consent
item.description: Denmark's culture minister will on Thursday propose a bill to ban the digital copying and sharing of lifelike representations of a person, including their appearance and voice, in a bid to crack down on the spread of AI-generated deepfakes.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Denmark's culture minister will on Thursday propose a bill to ban the digital copying and sharing of lifelike representations of a person, including their appearance and voice, in a bid to crack down on the spread of AI-generated deepfakes. Culture Minister Zenia Stampe said in a statement that AI manipulated videos and images could lead to misinformation and create doubt about what is real "One of the main goals of the bill is to get the tech giants to take down manipulated content quickly so that it causes as little harm as possible," she said The bill is meant to protect both the wider public and artists, whose performances and work may not be imitated and subsequently shared It does, however, include an exception for caricatures, parodies, satire and other work that criticises society and those in power The proposal is still subject to parliamentary approval Stampe said she hopes the bill will enter into force around the turn of year

item.title: Shares slip as oil jumps and bond yields stay high
item.description: Global shares slid on Thursday as a mild pullback in sovereign bond yields was countered by a jump in oil prices and indicators of the massive debt that technology companies may need to sustain their dramatic artificial intelligence-fueled growth.
item.dc:creator: Lawrence Delevingne, Marc Jones, Wayne Cole
item.content:encoded: Global shares slid on Thursday as a mild pullback in sovereign bond yields was countered by a jump in oil prices and indicators of the massive debt that technology companies may need to sustain their dramatic artificial intelligence-fueled growth. Wall Street's main indexes [USN:L6N45U189 TEXT:"fell"], with the S&P 500 (.SPX) down about 0.5% and the Nasdaq (.IXIC) off nearly 1.3%. Chipmakers (.SOX) , which have soared over 80% so far this year, were clear underperformers on the day following a report that OpenAI's annualized revenues were $20 billion less than the company previously signaled. Euro zone borrowing costs rose on Thursday as the surge in oil prices intensified inflation concerns, though investors [USN:L6N45U0ZV TEXT:"took a breather"] from selling bonds of heavily indebted countries such as France and Italy. The yield on benchmark US 10-year notes , also pulled back from its elevated levels, dipping 5 basis points to 5.227%. Yields started moving lower after a [USN:L1N45U0S2 TEXT:"30-year bond auction"] met with solid demand, showing investors remain willing to buy long-dated government debt, despite the ongoing market selloff. "Markets are going to be watchful if that contagion continues," said Kiran Ganesh, a multi-asset strategist at UBS Global Wealth Management. "At this stage, the markets would be most comforted by monetary intervention," he added, referring to the ECB buying bonds to ease the market strains. The pan-European STOXX 600 (.STOXX) [USN:L4N45U19A TEXT:"fell 0.75%"] to around its lowest since June, while France's CAC-40 (.FCHI) dropped 0.5%, nearing its lows for the year in March. Overnight in Asia, Japan's Nikkei (.N225) had shed 1.4% and South Korea's chipmaker-heavy KOSPI (.KS11) slumped 2.6%. AI DEBT RUSH In commodity markets, oil prices [USN:L1N45U031 TEXT:"settled 4% higher"], with Brent crude futures at $104.28, on revived concerns about the war in the Middle East and growing supply disruptions due to a hurricane approaching the US Gulf Coast. The US quarterly earnings season picks up pace next week with big banks, including JPMorgan (JPM.N) , set to report results. Optimism around strong earnings has buoyed US stocks lately despite shaky geopolitical developments and concerns about rising interest rates. The tech and energy sectors are expected to report the biggest quarterly earnings growth, while the broader S&P 500 (.SPX) is expected to post a punchy 30.6% increase in quarterly earnings, according to LSEG data. Vlad Barbalat, Liberty Mutual Group's chief investment officer and president of global risk & capital solutions, said the S&P 500’s roughly 15% return this year looks ordinary on the surface, but the composition is striking. "The index has risen even as its forward P/E has fallen from roughly 22x to 19x, supported by exceptionally strong growth in rolling forward earnings, all while more than a third of S&P 500 stocks are down," Barbalat wrote in an email. "The result is a historically uncommon combination: a narrow rally in which the market has gotten cheaper even as the index hovers near all-time highs." Debt remains a strong underwater current. The Wall Street Journal added to media reports on Wednesday that SpaceX (SPCX.O) , Broadcom (AVGO.O) and Oracle (ORCL.N) were all looking to raise serious money to buy high-end AI chips. Broadcom was looking for $50 billion in financing, while [USN:L6N45S1CR TEXT:"SpaceX"] was planning to issue $30 billion in investment-grade debt and raise $10 billion in loans to buy chips from Nvidia (NVDA.O) , which is a major shareholder in SpaceX. Credit default insurance on SpaceX jumped to record highs, while its shares and bonds lost ground. SOVEREIGN BONDS VS CORPORATE DEBT Still, the fact much of this money will be spent on AI equipment is set to be positive for earnings in the semiconductor and memory sectors. [USN:L1N45T115 TEXT:"Samsung Electronics"] (005930.KS) on Thursday reported a 783% jump in third-quarter operating profit to 107.4 trillion won ($80.17 billion), though its shares lost 2.4%. TSMC (2330.TW) , the world's largest contract chipmaker, also reported a [USN:L6N45U0AF TEXT:"record third-quarter revenue"] of T$1.49 trillion ($46.71 billion), up 50% from the year-earlier period. Its shares fell 1.35%. All this corporate debt is coming at a time when sovereign bond markets are being sorely tested by inflation fears, ever-widening budget deficits and rising cash rates. Minutes of the [USN:L6N45T0TQ TEXT:"Federal Reserve's"] last meeting released on Wednesday showed "most" members considered another rate hike likely by year-end, though they would approach each meeting with an open mind. Markets imply just a 17% chance the Fed will move again this month, but are nearly 83% priced for a rise in December. "We expect a second Fed hike in December, though we see a strong chance the Fed ultimately concludes further tightening is unnecessary," analysts at Goldman Sachs wrote in a note. Strains in the French bond market led [USN:L8N45T074 TEXT:"Bank of France head Emmanuel Moulin"] to say the country's economic situation was serious on Wednesday, but he said it did not need help from the European Central Bank. Still, the euro [USN:L6N45U16J TEXT:"gained"] against the dollar as a rise in euro zone bond yields stalled. The greenback also retreated versus the yen, with the Japanese currency protected by the threat of intervention. Non-interest-bearing gold has suffered as yields climbed, but it was [USN:L1N45U0FA TEXT:"steady"] at $4,111 an ounce having found bids at two-month lows.
